headline: P0054 (Family Practice, GA): elevated 99215 share, but sampled documentation largely supports billed levels
rationale: P0054 bills 99215 on 16.3% of 355 claims, against 4.2% expected for its patient complexity (risk-adjusted score 4.16, z 1.66). The excess shows up in every complexity stratum, including patients with 0 conditions (8.6% vs 2.1% for all providers) and 1 condition (11.2% vs 3.4%). Sampled low-complexity 99215s include single-condition hyperlipidemia visits (C0023651, C0023704, C0023769) and a 0-condition back-pain visit (C0023884). Even so, the records review does not support upcoding. Only 2 of 16 documented 99215 claims fell below the billed level (12.5%, about half the 24.2% all-provider rate). Lower levels also look clean: 0 of 17 99213 claims and 1 of 67 99214 claims were unsupported. One low-complexity 99215, C0023908 (asthma), was documented at moderate MDM and 31 minutes. Another, C0023971 (COPD), was documented at high MDM and 50 minutes. Supported 99215s include C0023666 and C0023724. Overall the pattern is more consistent with a legitimately complex workload than with upcoding. However, 16 documented 99215s is a modest sample, and the billing outlier among low-complexity patients is unexplained, so this conclusion is tentative. Diagnosis codes alone may understate acuity, but that is not verified.
next_steps: Pull records for more 99215 claims on 0-1 condition patients (e.g., C0023651, C0023704, C0023769, C0023884, C0023893, C0023958) to test whether the low-complexity excess is documented.
Review the two unsupported 99215s (C0023653, C0023908) to see whether the gap is borderline (moderate vs high MDM) or systematic.
Check whether billed levels rely on time and whether documented minutes meet 99215 thresholds consistently.
Compare acuity signals not captured in chronic-condition counts (acute problems, hospital follow-ups, diagnostic workups) for the low-complexity 99215 visits.
Re-run the screen with a larger documented sample before escalating or closing.
